item.text: {"chapter_id":"6B","answers":[{"question_id":"6B.1","answer":"Sisi’s government made welfare an explicit policy objective through Takaful and Karama, Haya Karima, social-protection increases, food-security planning, disability and labor commitments, and the 2023–2027 human-capital framework. Presidential announcements included emergency support for informal workers, higher transfers, minimum-wage measures, and protection for agricultural land and food security (BATCH-0021-E017; BATCH-0021-E018; BATCH-0022-E005; BATCH-0016-E001; BATCH-0019-E012; BATCH-0019-E015). Some programs had substantial operational reach: Takaful and Karama reportedly covered 4.67 million households by December 2023, and the system used conditional and unconditional benefits for children, older people, widows, orphans, and disabled people (BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0020-E013; BATCH-0020-E014). However, many commitments were announcements, plans, or externally supported frameworks rather than demonstrated executed budgets or enforceable rights (BATCH-0003-E010; BATCH-0013-E001; BATCH-0019-E012; BATCH-0019-E013). Adverse evidence indicates that austerity, megaproject spending, low social-pension spending, and inflation weakened welfare priority; poverty and basic-needs insecurity remained extensive (BATCH-0008-E004; BATCH-0009-R10-E006; BATCH-0009-R11-E004; BATCH-0015-E008; BATCH-0015-E009). Sisi’s September 2023 statement that hunger and deprivation could be acceptable sacrifices for development further qualifies the welfare orientation (BATCH-0001-E016). Attribution is strongest for presidential directives and weaker for collective government, donor, and World Bank programs; the evidence supports a mixed welfare purpose rather than a conclusively welfare-centered governing model.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-E017","BATCH-0021-E018","BATCH-0022-E005","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0020-E013","BATCH-0019-E015","BATCH-0016-E001"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0001-E016","BATCH-0008-E004","BATCH-0009-R10-E006","BATCH-0009-R11-E004","BATCH-0015-E008","BATCH-0015-E009","BATCH-0003-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Execution, budget disbursement, enforcement, and causal attribution are incomplete for many initiatives.","UN, World Bank, and donor-supported activity cannot be attributed solely to Sisi.","The evidence does not provide a complete welfare-budget portfolio for 2023."]},{"question_id":"6B.2","answer":"There is evidence of meaningful service-access expansion, especially through Takaful and Karama, Universal Health Insurance, social registries, World Bank-supported food-security measures, digital and transport infrastructure, and humanitarian medical arrangements (BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0020-E014; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0018-E004; BATCH-0019-E007). Universal Health Insurance had enrolled more than five million people in six Phase 1 governorates with over 322 accredited providers, although the figures are cumulative and not strictly year-end 2023 (BATCH-0023-E003). The government also reported conditional transfers for children and unconditional transfers for older people, widows, orphans, and persons with disabilities (BATCH-0020-E013). Access remained materially unequal or inadequate: nearly 30 percent lived in poverty, disadvantaged children and children with disabilities remained out of school, internet and service access varied sharply by region and socioeconomic status, and transfers covered only about one-third of families in or near poverty according to HRW’s assessment (BATCH-0005-E006; BATCH-0005-E007; BATCH-0009-R02-E006; BATCH-0009-R07-E010). Inflation, electricity cuts, reduced health and education spending, high service costs, and low-quality or fee-based provision impaired affordability and uptake (BATCH-0008-E004; BATCH-0009-R07-E011; BATCH-0008-E022; BATCH-0015-E008). The record demonstrates programs and some delivery, but not broad, affordable, effective, and equitable access across all listed domains.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0020-E013","BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0018-E004","BATCH-0019-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E006","BATCH-0005-E007","BATCH-0009-R02-E006","BATCH-0009-R07-E010","BATCH-0009-R07-E011","BATCH-0008-E004","BATCH-0015-E008","BATCH-0008-E022"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Coverage, quality, affordability, exclusion, and uptake are not consistently measured.","Housing, sanitation, water, food, and education evidence is fragmented and often not 2023-specific.","Shared donor and subnational implementation complicates ruler attribution."]},{"question_id":"6B.3","answer":"The government adopted or maintained formal measures for children, women, disabled people, older people, poor households, informal workers, refugees, and marginalized regions. Examples include Takaful and Karama eligibility for vulnerable groups, a five-percent disability employment directive, disability-accessibility rules, child-law amendments, anti-FGM and anti-trafficking institutions, scholarships for Upper Egypt, and proposed institutional strengthening for childhood and motherhood (BATCH-0020-E013; BATCH-0021-E018; BATCH-0024-R01-E018; BATCH-0002-E016; BATCH-0015-E007; BATCH-0019-E004). There were also some concrete protections and services, including cash-transfer reach, disability-related legal remedies, refugee health arrangements, and evacuation and treatment of children from Gaza (BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0024-R02-E002; BATCH-0018-E004; BATCH-0019-E007). Yet incidence and exclusion evidence is adverse: children with disabilities and refugee or migrant children remained out of school, child labor affected 4.2 million children including 3.7 million in hazardous work, gender-based violence and FGM remained widespread, and services for foreign and male trafficking victims were limited (BATCH-0005-E007; BATCH-0014-E010; BATCH-0011-E013; BATCH-0012-E022; BATCH-0008-E006). Sudanese refugees faced visa restrictions, arbitrary detention, harsh conditions, denial of asylum procedures, and forced return; North Sinai residents remained displaced without adequate return or compensation (BATCH-0007-E022; BATCH-0007-E023; BATCH-0004-E005; BATCH-0022-E011). Benefits were therefore targeted in form but incomplete in incidence, enforcement, and remedy.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E013","BATCH-0021-E018","BATCH-0024-R01-E018","BATCH-0002-E016","BATCH-0015-E007","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0018-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E007","BATCH-0014-E010","BATCH-0011-E013","BATCH-0012-E022","BATCH-0008-E006","BATCH-0007-E022","BATCH-0007-E023","BATCH-0004-E005","BATCH-0022-E011"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Group-level outcomes and regional incidence are incomplete.","Many favorable measures are government-reported, planned, or historically inherited rather than independently evaluated in 2023.","Personal presidential attribution is direct for some directives but only institutional for many programs."]},{"question_id":"6B.4","answer":"The record shows some administrative capacity, training, accreditation, digitalization, and service supervision. Universal Health Insurance had more than 322 accredited and contracted providers; anti-trafficking agencies trained thousands of officials and operated specialized prosecution and referral structures; Takaful and Karama used 15,000 social and community workers; recruitment bureaus were licensed, modernized, connected online, or revoked; and Sisi directed labor-market and employment institutions to develop platforms and training (BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0008-E007; BATCH-0020-E014; BATCH-0009-R04-E003; BATCH-0009-R04-E008; BATCH-0021-E019). Some enforcement occurred, such as the NTRA’s fine against Telecom Egypt and government-reported disciplinary measures against Interior Ministry personnel (BATCH-0002-E035; BATCH-0023-E014). However, the dominant administrative model relied heavily on military-managed projects with substantial autonomy in licensing, partner selection, and subcontracting, limited transparency, and weak evidence of professional civilian oversight (BATCH-0009-R10-E001; BATCH-0009-R10-E002; BATCH-0009-R10-E004). Service quality, staffing adequacy, procurement integrity, and patronage risks were not credibly resolved; military firms and regime-connected actors reportedly received no-bid contracts and privileged access, while social-service and anti-trafficking systems retained gaps and inconsistent victim identification (BATCH-0005-E010; BATCH-0008-E006; BATCH-0012-E023). The evidence supports pockets of competent administration within a politicized and opaque state structure.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0008-E007","BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0009-R04-E003","BATCH-0009-R04-E008","BATCH-0021-E019","BATCH-0002-E035"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-R10-E001","BATCH-0009-R10-E002","BATCH-0009-R10-E004","BATCH-0005-E010","BATCH-0008-E006","BATCH-0012-E023"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is no complete staffing, procurement, or executed-budget dataset for social services.","Training and accreditation are inputs and do not establish service quality or impartiality.","Evidence of qualified appointments is sparse and often concerns general state administration rather than welfare agencies."]},{"question_id":"6B.5","answer":"Egypt maintained some formal measurement, audit, and evaluation mechanisms: state budget documents were publicly accessible in part, Parliament listed audits, the social registry and health-expenditure tracking were developed, courts and ministries reported administrative performance, and the government described monitoring committees, human-rights strategies, and periodic reporting (BATCH-0002-E005; BATCH-0003-E002; BATCH-0018-E011; BATCH-0018-E012; BATCH-0009-R04-E001). Sisi also directed implementation studies for the National Dialogue and periodic reporting on investment and administrative reforms (BATCH-0019-E006; BATCH-0006-E021). Some corrections occurred, including Sisi’s pardon of Patrick Zaki, release of detainees, cancellation of one disciplinary referral, and court-ordered restoration of disability assistance (BATCH-0008-E027; BATCH-0009-R03-E010; BATCH-0009-R03-E011; BATCH-0024-R03-E016). Nevertheless, transparency was selective: military-enterprise debt and audits were withheld, military project data and environmental assessments were inaccessible, detention totals and investigations were unavailable, and independent monitoring access was restricted (BATCH-0002-E005; BATCH-0009-R10-E004; BATCH-0011-E014; BATCH-0023-E011). Independent assessments repeatedly found that the national dialogue, human-rights strategy, and pardon process produced limited or selective correction while repression continued (BATCH-0008-E013; BATCH-0008-E024; BATCH-0009-R03-E001; BATCH-0009-R03-E002). The evidence shows measurement and occasional correction, but weak transparency, independent evaluation, and systemic learning.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E005","BATCH-0018-E011","BATCH-0018-E012","BATCH-0009-R04-E001","BATCH-0019-E006","BATCH-0008-E027","BATCH-0009-R03-E010","BATCH-0024-R03-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-R10-E004","BATCH-0011-E014","BATCH-0023-E011","BATCH-0008-E013","BATCH-0008-E024","BATCH-0009-R03-E001","BATCH-0009-R03-E002","BATCH-0002-E005"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Many favorable data are official claims without independent verification.","Welfare-specific audits, impact evaluations, and documented corrective reallocations are scarce.","Information restriction makes absence of evidence difficult to interpret."]},{"question_id":"6B.6","answer":"The government undertook some crisis-preparedness and response measures: food-security interventions maintained bread subsidies during wheat-import disruption, emergency cash and social-protection measures were expanded, disaster and climate plans existed, Sinai reconstruction and development budgets were reported, Rafah facilitated food and medical aid, and Egypt established triage, ambulances, hospitals, and evacuation arrangements for Gaza patients (BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0022-E005; BATCH-0024-R02-E015; BATCH-0019-E008; BATCH-0019-E007; BATCH-0018-E004). Counterterrorism violence declined substantially in Sinai in 2023, although reporting was constrained (BATCH-0006-E009). These actions were partly effective or protective, but attribution is shared with international agencies and external partners, and many plans lack outcome evidence. Adverse evidence shows avoidable and unequal suffering: electricity cuts disrupted health care, water, and work and appeared longer in poor rural areas; inflation and food insecurity eroded protection; North Sinai displacement continued without return or compensation; residents protesting return were dispersed with live ammunition; Sudanese refugees were detained and forcibly returned without asylum safeguards (BATCH-0009-R07-E011; BATCH-0015-E008; BATCH-0022-E011; BATCH-0020-E007; BATCH-0004-E005). Historical Sinai operations involved demolitions, displacement, and alleged abuses, while the 2023 shift toward less-populated-area operations lacks independent civilian-protection evaluation (BATCH-0002-E023; BATCH-0006-E010). Crisis administration was therefore mixed: some preparation and humanitarian facilitation coexisted with austerity, unequal burdens, and coercive crisis management.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0019-E008","BATCH-0019-E007","BATCH-0018-E004","BATCH-0006-E009","BATCH-0024-R02-E015"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-R07-E011","BATCH-0015-E008","BATCH-0022-E011","BATCH-0020-E007","BATCH-0004-E005","BATCH-0002-E023","BATCH-0006-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is no comprehensive counterfactual estimate of avoidable deaths, deprivation, or unequal crisis harm.","Pandemic-era evidence is mostly historical and does not directly test 2023 preparedness.","External humanitarian actors and shocks materially complicate attribution."]},{"question_id":"6B.7","answer":"Formal rules included targeted eligibility for Takaful and Karama, constitutional equality guarantees, disability and labor protections, complaints and appeal mechanisms, administrative-court review, and legal authority for social institutions to receive complaints or assist victims (BATCH-0020-E013; BATCH-0024-R01-E008; BATCH-0024-R01-E016; BATCH-0024-R02-E016; BATCH-0024-R03-E016). Courts sometimes corrected administrative decisions, including disability-assistance and deportation-related measures, and Sisi’s pardon of Patrick Zaki and releases of detainees show limited corrective intervention (BATCH-0024-R02-E002; BATCH-0009-R04-E016; BATCH-0009-R03-E010). However, there is strong evidence that state benefits, permits, employment, housing, and basic security were vulnerable to political loyalty and punishment. Opposition supporters were arrested or obstructed during endorsement collection; critics and teachers were prosecuted under terrorism and false-news laws; detainees were recycled into new cases; NGOs faced registration pressure, asset restrictions, and closure; and private-sector and informal workers lacked binding wage enforcement or effective complaint protection (BATCH-0009-R03-E003; BATCH-0009-R03-E004; BATCH-0019-E022; BATCH-0011-E015; BATCH-0007-E021; BATCH-0021-E004). Selective pardon releases and repression of dialogue participants further indicate discretionary rather than neutral administration (BATCH-0009-R03-E002; BATCH-0009-R03-E001). Evidence specifically linking welfare eligibility decisions to partisan loyalty is thinner than evidence of political punishment in civic and employment administration, but the broader administrative environment did not reliably prevent politicization.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E013","BATCH-0024-R01-E008","BATCH-0024-R01-E016","BATCH-0024-R02-E002","BATCH-0024-R03-E016","BATCH-0009-R04-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-R03-E003","BATCH-0009-R03-E004","BATCH-0019-E022","BATCH-0011-E015","BATCH-0007-E021","BATCH-0021-E004","BATCH-0009-R03-E002","BATCH-0009-R03-E001"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Direct evidence on partisan allocation of ordinary welfare benefits is limited.","Formal eligibility rules cannot establish actual administrative neutrality.","Many appeal examples are historical and do not quantify 2023 access or compliance."]},{"question_id":"6B.8","answer":"Egypt retained formal constitutional equality and anti-discrimination provisions and enacted or maintained disability-accessibility rules, disability employment quotas, women’s institutions, anti-FGM measures, religious-site restoration, and some legal remedies (BATCH-0009-R05-E004; BATCH-0024-R01-E018; BATCH-0021-E018; BATCH-0002-E016; BATCH-0008-E029). There were practical positive actions, including disability court remedies, accessibility measures, treatment and evacuation of vulnerable children, and a presidential pardon for Patrick Zaki (BATCH-0024-R02-E002; BATCH-0024-R03-E013; BATCH-0019-E007; BATCH-0009-R03-E010). Yet enforcement and dignity outcomes were severely mixed. Women and girls faced widespread gender-based violence, FGM prevalence was reported at 86 percent among women aged 15–49, LGBTI people faced targeted arrests and detention abuse, Shia Muslims lacked public worship access, Christians reportedly faced pressured reconciliation, and children, migrants, refugees, and disabled people remained exposed to exclusion and violence (BATCH-0012-E021; BATCH-0012-E022; BATCH-0009-R07-E014; BATCH-0008-E029; BATCH-0008-E030; BATCH-0005-E007; BATCH-0014-E010). Sudanese refugees were detained and returned without individualized protection, while North Sinai residents were denied effective remedy for displacement and compensation (BATCH-0004-E005; BATCH-0022-E011). The record therefore shows formal protections and selective remedies alongside substantial practical discrimination, coercion, and dignity violations.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-R05-E004","BATCH-0024-R01-E018","BATCH-0021-E018","BATCH-0002-E016","BATCH-0024-R02-E002","BATCH-0009-R03-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-E021","BATCH-0012-E022","BATCH-0009-R07-E014","BATCH-0008-E029","BATCH-0008-E030","BATCH-0005-E007","BATCH-0014-E010","BATCH-0004-E005","BATCH-0022-E011"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Incidence data are uneven and often supplied by advocacy organizations or government reports.","The record does not establish uniform enforcement across regions or groups.","Personal presidential attribution is generally indirect except for selected directives and pardons."]},{"question_id":"6B.9","answer":"The government maintained or created several social institutions with formal mandates: Takaful and Karama and its dynamic registry, Universal Health Insurance, national councils for women, children and motherhood, persons with disabilities, and human rights, anti-trafficking committees, social-protection strategies, and the proposed National Council for Childhood and Motherhood (BATCH-0020-E014; BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0024-R01-E014; BATCH-0024-R01-E015; BATCH-0024-R04-E006; BATCH-0015-E007; BATCH-0012-E023). Some had statutory authority, budgets, professional staffing, training, data functions, complaint powers, or multiyear strategies (BATCH-0024-R01-E014; BATCH-0024-R04-E007; BATCH-0008-E007; BATCH-0023-E015). Institutions also demonstrated some resilience through continued cash transfers, health coverage expansion, humanitarian medical coordination, and anti-trafficking administration. Durability and independence are nevertheless uncertain. The proposed child-and-motherhood council was not shown to be enacted or funded; national strategies and councils often lacked independent oversight, reliable outcome evidence, or effective remedy; and military-managed projects operated with autonomy and limited transparency (BATCH-0015-E007; BATCH-0011-E010; BATCH-0009-R10-E001; BATCH-0009-R10-E004). External assessments found weak implementation capacity, insufficient funding, poor coordination, and limited civil-society participation, while political institutions remained subordinate to the executive (BATCH-0009-R10-E003; BATCH-0008-E002; BATCH-0008-E004). The evidence supports institutional layering and partial durability, not demonstrated independent, professional, and resilient social institutions beyond personal rule.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0024-R01-E014","BATCH-0024-R01-E015","BATCH-0024-R04-E006","BATCH-0008-E007","BATCH-0023-E015"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0015-E007","BATCH-0011-E010","BATCH-0009-R10-E001","BATCH-0009-R10-E004","BATCH-0009-R10-E003","BATCH-0008-E002","BATCH-0008-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Post-rule resilience cannot be observed because Sisi remained in office during the period.","Funding, staffing, independence, and implementation data are incomplete.","Several institutional claims come from government self-report or donor-supported programs."]},{"question_id":"6B.10","answer":"Some ordinary people ended 2023 with improved access or protection compared with earlier baselines: Takaful and Karama reached millions of households, Universal Health Insurance expanded in Phase 1 governorates, public transport improvements were associated with a reported 4 percent reduction in Greater Cairo air pollution, and selected health, housing, disability, and food-security programs delivered measurable outputs (BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0009-R10-E005; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0018-E007). These gains were partly attributable to state policy but also to World Bank, UN, and other partners, predecessor programs, and subnational implementation. Against them, poverty, inflation, food insecurity, unemployment, unequal access, child labor, and gender disparities remained severe: inflation approached 40 percent, poverty affected roughly one-third or more of the population depending on definition, transfers were inadequate for many households, electricity cuts harmed poor regions, 4.2 million children worked, and girls faced much higher unemployment (BATCH-0009-R07-E009; BATCH-0009-R07-E010; BATCH-0015-E008; BATCH-0014-E010; BATCH-0005-E008; BATCH-0007-E017). Megaproject debt, austerity, reduced health and education spending, weak service quality, displacement in North Sinai, refugee abuses, and unequal regional access limited durable life-chance improvement (BATCH-0008-E004; BATCH-0009-R10-E006; BATCH-0009-R10-E010; BATCH-0022-E011; BATCH-0009-R02-E006). External shocks from COVID-19, the Ukraine war, capital outflows, and climate and water stress materially worsened outcomes, but some policy choices amplified vulnerability (BATCH-0001-E013; BATCH-0001-E005; BATCH-0009-R10-E007; BATCH-0015-E008). The evidence supports simultaneous localized gains and broad deterioration or stagnation, with insufficient basis to claim durable, widely shared improvement attributable mainly to Sisi.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0009-R10-E005","BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0018-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-R07-E009","BATCH-0009-R07-E010","BATCH-0015-E008","BATCH-0014-E010","BATCH-0005-E008","BATCH-0007-E017","BATCH-0008-E004","BATCH-0009-R10-E006","BATCH-0009-R10-E010","BATCH-0022-E011","BATCH-0001-E013","BATCH-0001-E005","BATCH-0009-R10-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Comparable inherited-to-2023 outcome series are incomplete across health, education, housing, water, sanitation, and social protection.","Poverty and welfare estimates use differing definitions, dates, and sources.","Policy lag, donor financing, subnational delivery, demographic change, and external shocks prevent precise causal attribution."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["The evidence consistently shows a dual pattern: substantial formal welfare programs and selected measurable service gains coexist with austerity, high inflation, unequal access, weak quality, politicized administration, and severe dignity and rights violations.","Attribution is strongest for Sisi’s public directives, pardons, budgetary and strategic priorities, but weaker for collective ministries, donor-supported programs, World Bank operations, and inherited institutions.","The most consequential adverse evidence concerns distributional hardship, refugee and North Sinai treatment, detention conditions, discrimination, and the diversion or opacity of public resources; these qualify otherwise favorable program-level evidence.","Many positive records establish commitments, institutional structures, or outputs rather than verified outcomes, independent audits, beneficiary incidence, or durable post-rule effects."]}
